title: How FLYR helped an airline grow revenue by double digits
summary: Vamsi Kodam of FLYR on using multi-armed bandits to price airline seats, finding wins hidden in tied results, and testing human overrides against automation.
body_markdown:
Airline seats are the definition of perishable inventory. Once the flight takes off, an empty seat can never be sold, and the same seat can never be sold twice.[On this episode of The Experimentation Edge](https://www.growthbook.io/podcast/episode/2-13) ,[Vamsi Kodam](https://www.growthbook.io/podcast/guests/vamsi-kodam) , Senior Director of Product Management at FLYR, told host Ashley Stirrup how experimentation helps airlines price and package that inventory, and why some of his most valuable tests never produced a clear winner.


## A modern commerce platform for airlines


FLYR is a Series D travel technology company building a modern commerce platform for airlines. Much of the technology airlines run on was built decades ago, Vamsi said, and a good part of it predates the internet. FLYR is building for the retailing era instead: a consumer-centric, personalized experience that helps airlines serve their customers better.


It is an enterprise product, or as Vamsi put it, B to B to C. Riyadh Air, the new flagship airline launched by the Saudi government, adopted FLYR's platform instead of a decades-old passenger service system. One visible difference is a cart. On most airline websites, if you shop, leave and come back, the site has lost the context of what you were looking for. On Riyadh Air you can put options in a cart, come back to them, and the platform learns your preferences over time.


Vamsi leads FLYR's offer and optimization suite. That covers the product catalog, which defines everything an airline can sell beyond the seat from A to B; the pricing engine, with all its nuance and complexity; and offer orchestration, which takes every request, checks the catalog and pricing engine, and returns a personalized response in milliseconds.


## The man versus machine test


Vamsi started his career as a data scientist and ran his first A/B test 15 to 16 years ago, for an airline that used automated decision systems to set prices. The system weighed demand, remaining capacity, time of day and many other variables, and sent price recommendations straight to the platform. Analysts sat in the loop, reviewing recommendations and intervening when something looked off.


The question was simple: how much value were those human interventions adding, or were they taking value away? Vamsi designed what the team called a “man versus machine” test, or more precisely, man plus machine versus machine. On some days the system ran untouched. On the rest, analysts adjusted as usual.


Vamsi had a strong hunch about the outcome. The model used an exponential price elasticity curve, and he believed it was wrong at the edges. Dropping a fare from $50 to $40 can move demand, but nobody's decision changes between $5,000 and $5,200. He expected a logistic, sigmoid-shaped curve and was worried the machine-only days would dilute revenue.


## A tie that taught the team the most


The result surprised him. Across the whole network, revenue was more or less the same with or without human intervention. But when the team sliced the data by point of sale, the picture changed. In some parts of the network, human intervention made more revenue. In others, it made no difference. And in some, the system alone would have done a better job.


“It was not like a win or lose, right? It's actually a learning of how you interact,” Vamsi said. The team turned those patterns into guidelines for when analysts should intervene, implemented them and ran another round of A/B testing. One of the biggest gaps came from an intervention an analyst had set up for an event and then forgot to remove, so it kept applying unnoticed.


The experience shaped how Vamsi works. “There's nothing like a failed experiment, I would say. There's always a learning.” When he hears a best practice or a strong intuition, “I would not take it on faith but I've learned to question and kind of think about it from first principles,” and collect data to back the decision.


Ashley connected the story to his own experience at a supply chain startup, where statistics repeatedly showed that people ordering by gut introduced inconsistency and cost. Vamsi framed the balance as 80/20 or 90/10: a well-designed system should handle most decisions, while humans handle the edge cases and guardrails.


## Multi-arm bandits and double-digit revenue


At FLYR, Vamsi's team applied reinforcement learning to a pricing problem where there was no historical data to start from. They used a multi-arm bandit: create multiple variants, send traffic through them, learn which ones win, and route more traffic to the winners.


The biggest difference from a traditional A/B test is speed. “With a multi-arm bandit the advantage is that you don't have to wait for the experiment to conclude,” Vamsi said. The bandit keeps testing the other arms too, so if behavior shifts, it adapts. The result: “The airline has seen double-digit revenue improvement for the problem.”


Because FLYR's products sit behind airline websites, all of an airline's consumer traffic hits them, thousands of requests per second answered in 20 to 30 milliseconds. Experimentation is built into what FLYR offers its airline partners, not just how FLYR builds software.


## Start with what others already learned


Asked how he designs experiments to learn as much as possible, Vamsi pointed to research. Before starting any new problem, he looks for academic and practitioner literature and technical blogs from companies that have faced something similar. “We can't be the first ones to be facing this problem,” he said. That gives him an intuition before the first test runs, so he can go from zero to one faster. He recently studied how DoorDash rolled out multi-arm bandits. “There's a lot to pick from what others are doing and you don't have to do everything on your own.”


Keeping up used to be hard for a busy product leader. Now Vamsi has AI bots set up to monitor new content and send him summaries.


## The next frontier: experimenting on the product


Airlines have historically focused their rigor on price. Vamsi sees the next opportunity in the product itself. Today most airline sites show the same three or four fare options regardless of context. A family booking a week-long vacation two months out has different needs than a business traveler flying out for two days next week. FLYR has laid the groundwork in its commerce platform, and over the next 1 to 2 years Vamsi wants to build the product side of experimentation, learn from it and iterate.


AI is already changing how fast his team ships. Work that used to take a year or two now gets done in about a quarter, freeing the team to tackle tech debt and features that would otherwise wait. Ashley noted that this is exactly why GrowthBook customers wrap every new feature in a feature flag: moving fast is safer with an automatic rollback when something breaks, especially in an industry like air travel.


The lesson from Vamsi's career is consistent. Question the intuition, test it, slice the results, and treat every outcome as a learning.
